lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Antisthenes, Crates — we've got some free time. Why don't we take a stroll right up to the descent and watch the new arrivals? See what kind of shape they're in and what they're up to.

lines.speaker: Antisthenes
lines.text: Let's go. It should be a pleasant spectacle — seeing some of them in tears, others begging to be let go, some dragging their heels on the way down, Hermes pushing them by the scruff of the neck while they lean back with all their might. [Laughs] Entirely pointless, of course.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Well, I can tell you what I saw on the road when I came down.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Do tell, Crates. You look like you saw something absolutely ridiculous.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: There was a big crowd coming down with me, but the most distinguished were Ismenodorus, our local rich man; Arsaces, the governor of Media; and Oroetes the Armenian. Ismenodorus had been murdered by bandits around Mount Cithaeron on his way to Eleusis. He was groaning, clutching his wound with both hands, calling out for the infants he'd left behind, and blaming himself for his own stupidity. Crossing Cithaeron and going through the Eleutherae region — completely deserted because of the wars — taking only two slaves with him. And doing all this while carrying five gold bowls and four cups!

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: As for Arsaces — an old man, and to be fair, quite dignified-looking — he was fuming in that barbarian way of his. He was outraged that he had to walk on foot, and kept demanding they bring his horse. You see, the horse had died with him. They were both skewered by a single blow from a Thracian peltast in a skirmish on the Araxes. Arsaces was charging, as he told it, having ridden far out ahead of his lines. The Thracian stood his ground, deflected the lance with his buckler, then set his own pike and skewered both man and horse.

lines.speaker: Antisthenes
lines.text: How is it possible, Crates, for that to happen with a single blow?

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Very easily, Antisthenes. Arsaces was charging with a thirty-foot lance. The Thracian parries the thrust, lets the point pass him, drops to one knee, and catches the charge on his pike. He wounds the horse right under the chest, and the horse impales itself through sheer momentum and fury. Arsaces is run right through from the groin straight out the buttocks. So you see, it was more the horse's doing than the man's. He was furious nonetheless. Being a Peer of the Realm, he expected to ride down to the underworld on horseback.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Oroetes, meanwhile, was so tender in the feet he couldn't even stand on the ground, let alone walk. It’s exactly what happens to all Medes when they dismount — they tiptoe along like they're walking on thorns. So when he threw himself down and absolutely refused to get up, our excellent Hermes just picked him up and carried him all the way to the ferry. I just laughed.

lines.speaker: Antisthenes
lines.text: When I came down, I didn't even mix with the rest of them. I left them wailing, sprinted down to the ferry, and bagged a seat to make sure I had a comfortable crossing. During the voyage they were all weeping and getting seasick. I had a lovely time enjoying the show.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Well, Crates, Antisthenes, those were the traveling companions you happened to get. My descent-buddies were Blepsias the moneylender from Pisa, Lampis the Acarnanian mercenary captain, and Damis the rich man from Corinth. Damis was poisoned by his son; Lampis slit his own throat for the love of Myrtium the courtesan; and Blepsias, the wretched creature, was said to have starved to death. He certainly looked it — deathly pale and emaciated to the absolute limit. Even though I already knew, I questioned them about how they died. Then, as Damis started blaming his son, I said, 'To be perfectly honest, you didn't suffer any injustice from him. You were ninety years old, sitting on a thousand talents and living in luxury, and you gave an eighteen-year-old kid a four-obol allowance.' 'And you, Acarnanian,' I said — he was groaning too, cursing Myrtium — 'why blame Love when you should blame yourself? You never once trembled before the enemy, you fought recklessly on the front lines, but the great hero gets captured by an ordinary little tart with fake tears and sighs!' Blepsias had already beaten me to it and was calling himself a total idiot for hoarding his money for completely unrelated heirs, vainly thinking he'd live forever. Anyway, listening to them groan gave me no ordinary amount of pleasure.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: But here we are at the entrance. We should look out and spot the arrivals from a distance. [Pauses, looking] Wow. A huge, mixed crowd, and every single one of them crying — except for the babies and toddlers. Even the incredibly old men are wailing! What is this? Does the love potion of life really have such a hold on them?

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: I'm going to ask this superannuated fossil. [To the Pauper] Why are you crying about dying at your age? Why are you upset, my good man, arriving as an old man? Let me guess, you were a king?

lines.speaker: Pauper
lines.text: Not at all.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: A satrap, then?

lines.speaker: Pauper
lines.text: Not that either.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Ah, so you were rich, and it pains you to die and leave behind a life of great luxury?

lines.speaker: Pauper
lines.text: Nothing of the sort. I was about ninety years old. I scratched out a miserable living with a fishing rod and line. I was exceptionally poor, childless, and on top of that, lame and half-blind.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And being in that state, you still wanted to live?

lines.speaker: Pauper
lines.text: Yes. The light was sweet. And dying is terrible. It's something to be avoided.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: You're out of your mind, old man. You're behaving like a teenager about destiny, and you're the same age as the ferryman! [To the others] What can anyone possibly say about the youth, when people this old are so in love with life? You'd think they'd be chasing death down as the cure for the evils of old age. Let's get out of here, before someone sees us loitering around the mouth of the underworld and thinks we're plotting an escape.
